blocks.html: In this case, it seems that a proof by rumour and common repute ought not to be of small force: for we are in a matter most ambiguous, monstrous and perplexed; in which acts, inasmuch as the certainty of things cannot be recovered except with great difficulty, rumour and common repute make sufficient proof a: as to show that Antoine is the son of Pierre, or that François is the son of Jean, or any other filiation b; or indeed to prove the death of someone.

notes.citation: The Doctors (commentators) on Decretals X 2.20.10 (De testibus et attestationibus, c. Veniens ad nos cum litteris tuis L. presbyter, the first of the two chapters so beginning in the title; the other is c. 38) and X 2.20.27, c. Praeterea (Celestine III: carnal union proved by hearsay testimony where fama and other aids concur)
notes.original: Les Docteurs au c. veniens. i. & au c. præterea. de teſtibus.
notes.gloss: The canonists' doctrine that in matters hard to prove directly, common repute (fama) suffices; c. Praeterea, de testibus is one of the marginalia decoded in the case file §6.3.

notes.citation: Decretals X 2.19.10 (De probationibus, c. Per tuas: one commonly reputed a man's son, and acknowledged by him, is not disowned by his later oath)
Bartolus (Bartole) on Digest 29.3.2.4 (Testamenta quemadmodum aperiantur, inspiciantur et describantur, l. 2, § Si dubitetur; Ulpian)
notes.original: Bartole en la. ij. P. ſi dubitetur. D. quẽ ad. teſt. aper,
notes.gloss: Bartolus there discusses how the death of a testator is proved, and admits proof by common repute. The P. stands for the paragraph sign; the note ends with a comma in the print.
